html:
The potato reached Europe from the Andes of South America around 1570, carried by the Spanish. Over the next two centuries it became a staple across much of Europe and helped feed a great rise in population.

The potato was first domesticated in the highlands of southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia some 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. Andean farmers grew hundreds of varieties, adapted to cold and altitude, and freeze-dried them into chuño for storage. It was a core food of the Inca Empire.

Spanish conquerors met it in the 1530s, and by about 1570 potatoes were grown in Spain, probably first in the Canary Islands. It was part of the Columbian Exchange. Acceptance was slow. Many Europeans thought it was food for animals or the poor, and some feared it caused disease, since it is related to poisonous nightshade.

From the late 1600s and 1700s it spread (see potato spreads in Europe):

  • In Ireland it became the main food of the poor.
  • In Prussia, Frederick the Great pressed farmers to plant it after famines.
  • In France, Antoine Parmentier promoted it in the 1770s and 1780s.

A small field of potatoes gave far more food than grain, and it grew in poor soil. Historians link it to the population boom that fed Europe's cities and industrialisation. Dependence on one crop was dangerous, though: in Ireland, potato blight caused the Great Famine of 1845 to 1852, with about a million dead and a million more emigrating.
sum: The potato reached Europe from the Andes of South America around 1570, carried by the Spanish. Over the next two centuries it became a staple across much of Europe and helped feed a great rise in population.
